extracted.intended_audience: students of Math 216 / learners of algebraic geometry (graduate or advanced undergraduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpts from Ravi Vakil's Foundations of Algebraic Geometry (Math 216) covering Serre's criterion and related commutative-algebra facts, the 27 lines on a cubic surface (classification and configuration), and cohomology & base-change theorems. Intended as textbook material with statements, proofs, and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular local rings are integrally closed
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular local rings are integrally closed. Serre’s criterion can be used to show this without invoking the harder fact that they are UFDs; regular local rings are Cohen–Macaulay and regular in codimension 0, and one only needs regularity in codimension 1 to conclude integral closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Serre's criterion and facts about localizations of regular local rings; for finitely generated algebras over a perfect field, localization preserves regularity (see referenced Facts and Exercises).

rubrics_metrics.name: S2 is a condition on all primes
rubrics_metrics.description: The condition S2 (Serre's condition) is a condition on all primes of the ring, not just those of codimension at most 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautionary remark: showing S2 at small-codimension primes is not sufficient; Exercise 26.3.E asks for an example satisfying R1 and Cohen–Macaulay at points of codimension ≤2 but not normal, illustrating the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal implies R1 + S2 (one direction of Serre's criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is normal (and hence all localizations are normal), then A satisfies R1 and S2: it is reduced (hence S1) and satisfies R1 by Theorem 12.5.8; to check S2 one shows that a normal Noetherian local ring (A,m) of dimension >1 has depth at least 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch provided: pick nonzero x ∈ m and show depth A/(x) > 0 via associated primes and use integrally closed hypothesis, Hartogs-type argument (Algebraic Hartogs's Lemma 11.3.10) to get required inclusions in localizations at codimension 1 primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: R1 + S2 implies normal (Serre's criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (A,m) is a Noetherian local ring satisfying R1 and S2 (and hence R0 and S1), then A is integrally closed (normal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof proceeds by reducing to the integral domain case (easier) and then handling the general reduced case via showing A is integrally closed in its total fraction ring and applying a lemma decomposing R into integrally closed integral domains (Lemma 26.3.11). Several exercises (26.3.F–I, 26.3.G, 26.3.H) guide the steps; inductive arguments on dimension are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral-domain case of R1 + S2 → normal
rubrics_metrics.description: When A is an integral domain and x ∈ K(A) is integral over A, write x = f/g with g a non-zerodivisor and show f ∈ (g) using S2 and R1 hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument uses a monic equation for f/g, inductive dimension reduction via non-zerodivisors, and depth comparisons (depth A ≥ 2 implies depth A/(g) ≥ 1) to conclude integrality forces membership in A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: integrally closed in total fraction ring ⇒ product of integrally closed domains
rubrics_metrics.description: If R is reduced with finitely many minimal primes p1, …, pn and R is integrally closed in its total fraction ring, then R is a finite product of integrally closed integral domains (R ≅ ∏ Rei).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses idempotents in the total fraction ring and that integrality closure forces R to contain the idempotents isolating each minimal-prime factor; Exercises 26.3.H–I guide the construction and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every smooth cubic surface has exactly 27 lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 27.1.1: Every smooth cubic surface in P3_k has exactly 27 lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proof uses the incidence correspondence Z ⊂ G(1,3)×P19 parametrizing lines contained in cubics, shows Z→P19 is finite and flat over the open locus of smooth cubics (P19\Δ), uses the reducedness of points in fibers (Theorem 27.3.1) so each line counts with multiplicity 1, and compares with the Fermat cubic (which has 27 lines) to get the constant count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every smooth cubic surface is P2 blown up at six points
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 27.1.2: Every smooth cubic surface over k is isomorphic to P2 blown up at six points (with appropriate genericity conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct two disjoint lines on X (Exercise 27.3.J), project from each to get a birational map to P1×P1 that contracts five lines; contracting those (Castelnuovo's criterion) and reversing blow-ups yields P2 blown up at six points. Exercises 27.4.A–E give details and constraints on the six points (distinct, no three collinear, not all on a conic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminant hypersurface ∆ in parameter space of cubics
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an irreducible hypersurface Δ ⊂ P19 whose closed points correspond precisely to singular cubic surfaces over k; Δ is irreducible of codimension 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct incidence correspondence Y parametrizing (cubic surface X, singular point p) and project to P19; show Y is a P15-bundle over P3 (hence irreducible of dimension 18) and its image is Δ (Exercises 27.2.A, 27.2.E–G).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidence correspondence Z properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Z ⊂ G(1,3)×P19 parametrizing (line ℓ ⊂ P3, cubic surface X) such that ℓ ⊂ X is an irreducible smooth variety of dimension 19 (a P15-bundle over G(1,3)), and the projection π: Z→P19 is projective and surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use local descriptions of the Grassmannian and linear conditions for a line to lie on a cubic; Exercises 27.3.A–B guide showing Z is P15-bundle and dimensions of fibers, and that most cubics have finitely many lines by upper semicontinuity of fiber dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: No first-order deformations of a line on a smooth cubic surface
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 27.3.1: If ℓ is a line in a regular cubic surface X then {ℓ} is a reduced point of the fiber of π (i.e., a line in a smooth cubic surface has no first-order deformations as a subscheme of X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to a local calculation: parameterize nearby lines by (a,a',b,b') coordinates, substitute into the cubic equation, and use regularity conditions (nonvanishing of certain linear/quadratic coefficients Cx(t), Cy(t)) to force the linearized coordinates to vanish. Exercises 27.3.C–E lead through the calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Z→P19 is finite étale of degree 27 over smooth locus
rubrics_metrics.description: Over P19\Δ (the locus of smooth cubics), π: Z→P19 is finite and flat; combining finiteness, flatness, and Theorem 27.3.1 gives that π is finite étale of degree 27 away from Δ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use that fibers are 0-dimensional over P19\Δ (π finite there), Z regular and P19 regular imply Miracle Flatness (26.2.11) so π is flat, and reducedness of points in fibers gives multiplicity one for each point; compare with Fermat example to determine degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Configuration of 27 lines and its constancy
rubrics_metrics.description: The intersection/configuration data of the 27 lines is the same for all smooth cubic surfaces: there is a finite étale cover parametrizing an ordered list of 27 distinct lines, so the incidence pattern (which pairs intersect) is constant across the smooth locus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the 27th fibered power of Z over P19\Δ to parametrize ordered lists of 27 lines, then restrict to the open-and-closed locus where lines are distinct (Exercise 27.3.F). Use monodromy and connectedness arguments (Exercises 27.3.G–I) to transport the Fermat configuration to any smooth cubic; symmetry group is W(E6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weyl group symmetry of the 27-line configuration
rubrics_metrics.description: The subgroup of permutations of the 27 lines preserving intersection data is the Weyl group W(E6) (order 51840); the Galois group of the Galois closure of K(Z)/K(P19\Δ) is isomorphic to W(E6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remark 27.3.5 points to verification using the Fermat surface and computation of the degree of the appropriate finite étale cover; see references for full group-theoretic identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of lines via (-1)-curves
rubrics_metrics.description: On a smooth cubic surface X, a curve C⊂X is a line iff C is a (−1)-curve (Definition 20.2.6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the adjunction formula (and referenced exercises) to check the numerical conditions; Exercise 27.2.C gives the hint to use adjunction and earlier exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constraints for blowing up P2 to obtain a smooth cubic surface
rubrics_metrics.description: Blowing up P2 at six points yields a smooth cubic surface embedded anticanonically in P3 only if the six points are distinct, no three are collinear, and they are not all on a conic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 27.4.D and 27.4.E show how special configurations create exceptional curves with (KX·C) ≥ 0, obstructing an anticanonical embedding as a cubic; Proposition 27.4.3 outlines that for the allowed configurations the anticanonical linear series gives a closed embedding into P3 as a cubic surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticanonical embedding of smooth cubic surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Any smooth cubic surface X ⊂ P3 is anticanonically embedded: the embedding is given by the anticanonical linear series K_X^∨.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 27.2.B indicates using the adjunction formula to verify the anticanonical embedding property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three desiderata for cohomology in proper flat families
rubrics_metrics.description: Given π: X→Y proper with F coherent on X flat over Y, three desirable properties are: (a) fiberwise base-change isomorphism φ_p^q: (R^pπ_*F)⊗κ(q) → H^p(X_q,F|X_q); (b) for any base change ψ: Z→Y, φ_p^Z: ψ^*(R^pπ_*F) → R^pπ'_*(ψ'^*F) is an isomorphism; (c) R^pπ_*F is locally free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties are closely related; proving them requires semi-continuity/Grauert-type results and flatness hypotheses. Flat base change (Theorem 24.2.8) already gives (a)/(b) when ψ is flat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Semicontinuity Theorem for cohomology (28.1.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose π: X→Y is proper between Noetherian schemes and F is a coherent sheaf on X flat over Y. Then for each p the function q↦dim_{κ(q)} H^p(X_q, F|X_q) is upper semicontinuous on Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translation: cohomology dimensions of fibers vary upper semicontinuously in proper flat families. Use this to deduce that checking constancy on a quasicompact Y reduces to checking closed points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grauert's theorem on cohomology and base change (28.1.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X→Y is proper, Y is reduced and locally Noetherian, F coherent on X flat over Y, and h^p(X_q,F|X_q) is a locally constant function of q∈Y, then R^pπ_*F is locally free and for every ψ: Z→Y the base-change map φ_p^Z is an isomorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus locally constant fiber dimension (over a reduced base) is a sufficient condition to glue fiber cohomology into a vector bundle and have base-change isomorphisms. No Noetherian hypotheses on Y are needed in the statement beyond 'locally Noetherian'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and typical loci of local freeness
rubrics_metrics.description: By Semicontinuity, on an integral base Y there exists a dense open subset where R^pπ_*F is locally free (and base-change holds); more generally, if ψ is flat then cohomology commutes with base change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Semicontinuity Theorem together with upper-semicontinuity of ranks and Miracle Flatness-type results; references to Theorem 24.2.8 (flat base change) and Theorem 24.7.1 (constancy of Euler characteristic for flat families) are given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohomology can jump in positive characteristic; H^0(O) constant in char 0 for smooth families
rubrics_metrics.description: In characteristic 0, cohomology of O in smooth families does not jump (Betti numbers constant, and Hodge-theoretic decomposition gives constancy of H^j(Ω^i)). However, cohomology of O can jump in positive characteristic (examples referenced).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Hodge theory over C and Lefschetz principle to reduce general char 0 cases; counterexamples in positive characteristic (and the necessity of smoothness hypotheses) are highlighted by earlier examples (24.4.13).
